title: Tokenization Impacts Multilingual Language Modeling: Assessing Vocabulary Allocation and Overlap Across Languages
problem_statement: Investigating the influence of subword tokenization properties—specifically vocabulary allocation (representing language-specific lexical units) and vocabulary overlap (sharing lexical units across languages)—on multilingual language model representations and downstream task performance.
domain: Multilingual natural language processing, subword tokenization, and cross-lingual representation learning across diverse language families and writing systems.
theoretical_framework: Multilingual Transformer language models allocate a large proportion of parameters in the input embedding layer. The lexical representations learned by subword tokenizers determine the trade-off between cross-lingual parameter sharing (vocabulary overlap) and language-specific capacity (vocabulary allocation), which can be evaluated by probing frozen contextual representations.
methodology: The authors introduced non-parametric metrics to evaluate tokenizers: Vocabulary Allocation measured via Average Rank (AR) and Characters Per Token (CPT), and Vocabulary Overlap measured via Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD). They compared SentencePiece Unigram LM, BPE, and two novel merging methods (NOOVERLAP and TOKMIX). They pre-trained scaled-down XLM-RoBERTa models (150M parameters) on balanced Common Crawl subsets (6 and 20 languages) and evaluated representations using masked language modeling (MRR) and frozen linear probing across word-level and sentence-level downstream tasks.
datasets: CC-100 (Common Crawl 10% balanced subsample for pre-training across 6 and 20 languages)
Universal Dependencies (UD) for Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging and Dependency Tree Labeling
Tatoeba bitext corpus for cross-lingual sentence retrieval

model_metrics: Masked Language Modeling Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)
Macro-averaged F1 score for word-level tasks (POS tagging, NER, Dependency edge labeling)
Cosine similarity alignment accuracy for sentence retrieval (Tatoeba)
evaluation.statistical_analysis: Spearman rank correlation coefficients (with p-values) computed across multiple random seeds.

key_findings: High vocabulary allocation (higher average rank and longer characters per token) significantly improves in-language results and cross-lingual transfer for word-level downstream tasks including POS tagging, NER, and dependency labeling.

Vocabulary overlap across languages benefits cross-lingual transfer for sentence-level semantic tasks (XNLI, Tatoeba sentence retrieval) and NER within the same script, but impairs performance on syntactic tasks (POS tagging and dependency labeling).

Completely eliminating vocabulary overlap (NOOVERLAP) achieves superior performance on POS tagging and dependency labeling among same-script languages, showing that shared surface strings with distinct cross-lingual meanings introduce negative interference for syntactic tasks.

Higher masked language modeling performance (MRR) negatively correlates with word-level downstream task performance because higher vocabulary allocation increases the candidate prediction space during masked pre-training while providing richer lexical features for downstream tasks.

Standard SentencePiece Unigram LM underperforms BPE and TOKMIX in multilingual vocabulary allocation, as its character n-gram initialization restricts vocabulary coverage for larger vocabulary sizes across most languages except Chinese.
scope_and_delimitations: Investigated a primary set of 6 typologically diverse languages (Arabic, Chinese, Greek, Turkish, Spanish, English) and extended to a broader set of 20 languages.
Pre-trained scaled-down XLM-RoBERTa architectures (8 layers, 6 attention heads, hidden dimension 768, 150M parameters) with a fixed vocabulary size of 120,000.
Evaluated representations via linear probes on frozen contextualized embeddings rather than full fine-tuning.
Pre-training was conducted on a 10% balanced sample of CC-100 data with an exponential smoothing parameter alpha = 0.25.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: To achieve robust, unbiased results, we decided to train first on a smaller number of languages, fix our methodology and then confirm our findings on the full set of languages. This meant that two rounds of pretraining needed to be done and because of that, we scaled our models down for computational efficiency reasons. Another limitation of our methodology is the choice to train linear probes on top of the contextualized word representations instead of the more common finetuning approach. Nevertheless, we think that probing gives better insight into the pretrained model's representation.
limitations.summary: The authors used scaled-down language models with 150M parameters to manage computational costs across multiple pre-training iterations, and evaluated the models using frozen linear probes rather than full end-to-end fine-tuning.

generalizability_gap: The empirical findings are based on scaled-down 150M parameter models evaluated on up to 20 languages, which leaves uncertain whether the observed trade-offs between vocabulary allocation and overlap persist identically in large-scale foundation models (such as models with >300M to hundreds of billions of parameters) or across extremely low-resource languages.
methodological_gap: The evaluation methodology relies exclusively on linear probing of frozen embeddings rather than full task-specific fine-tuning or parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), and the NOOVERLAP method could not be scaled to 20 languages due to per-language vocabulary partition constraints.
future_work: Identifying optimal multilingual tokenization and vocabulary construction strategies to balance language-specific representation and cross-lingual sharing.
Evaluating vocabulary allocation and overlap dynamics in larger-scale multilingual language models.
Investigating tokenization behavior and vocabulary allocation on broader collections of low-resource languages and scripts.
Comparing linear probing insights with full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient adaptation methods.
